rows.question: How does CUPED reduce noise in experiments?
rows.answer: CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) reduces noise by using each user's behaviour before the experiment. rows.question: Why is checking the dashboard every day and stopping early dangerous?
rows.answer: A fixed-horizon test is valid only if you look at the p-value once, at the planned end. [1] If you check every day and stop the first time p < 0.05, you give chance many opportunities to cross the threshold, so the false positive rate rises well above 5%. [1] In 1,000 simulated A/A tests (no real effect) with 14 daily looks, a single check at the end gave false positives 5.0% of the time, but stopping at the first daily p < 0.05 produced a false positive in 11.9% of tests, more than double the promised rate. rows.question: How many users per arm do I need to detect a 3% change in watch time?
rows.answer: To detect a relative lift (minimum detectable effect, MDE) with significance level alpha and power 1 - beta, each arm needs n = 2 (z_(1-alpha/2) + z_(1-beta))^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2 users, where sigma is the metric's standard deviation and delta = baseline mean * MDE. [2] In the control groups of past LIVE experiments, watch time averages about 74 minutes per user over 14 days with a standard deviation of about 115 minutes, because a few heavy viewers watch for hours. [1] Detecting a 3% relative lift with 80% power at the 5% level therefore needs about 41,900 users per arm without CUPED, and about 22,400 per arm with CUPED. [1] The formula was tested by simulation: for a 3% lift it asked for 30,511 users per arm on the simulated metric, and in 500 simulated tests of exactly that size the test was significant 79.4% of the time, matching the promised 80% power. [3]
